content.overview: Section 3 of the Limitation Act, 1963 is the bar. Subject to sections 4 to 24, every suit instituted, appeal preferred, and application made after the prescribed period shall be dismissed, although limitation has not been set up as a defence. The court applies the bar. A defendant need not plead it. The prescribed period is the period in the Schedule for that suit, appeal or application. Sections 4 to 24 are the only statutory reasons to compute or extend time differently.
content.study: Find the Schedule article and the starting point first. Then ask whether any of sections 4 to 24 changes the count. Do not wait for a plea. Do not use section 5 to save a late suit.

learningObjectives: Note that limitation need not be pleaded.
Keep sections 4 to 24 as the only statutory qualifications.
enhancement.definition: Section 3 requires dismissal of a suit, appeal or application filed after the prescribed period, even if limitation is not pleaded.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Limitation is a court-applied bar, not a defence that is waived by silence. The bar is subject only to sections 4 to 24.
enhancement.statutoryFramework: Limitation Act, 1963, section 3, read with the Schedule and sections 4 to 24.
essentialIngredients: Proceeding is a suit, appeal or application
Prescribed period identified from the Schedule
Institution, preferring or making is after that period
No section 4 to 24 exclusion or extension is made out
Dismissal although limitation was not pleaded
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 3(1) is mandatory in form. The court dismisses a late suit, appeal or application. The words 'although limitation has not been set up as a defence' mean the bar is not left to the defendant. Section 3(2) treats a claim by way of set-off or a counter-claim as a separate suit, instituted when the set-off or counter-claim is pleaded, and on the same date as the suit in which it is pleaded for limitation against that claim. The section does not choose the period. The Schedule does. It also does not condone delay. Condonation of appeals and applications is section 5, and that section does not apply to suits or to Order XXI applications.
examples: A money suit is filed one day after the Schedule period. The defendant does not plead limitation. Section 3 still requires dismissal unless a sections 4 to 24 rule applies.
A counter-claim is pleaded after the period for that claim. Section 3(2) treats it as a separate suit.
An appeal is late but sufficient cause is shown. Section 3 is subject to section 5.
enhancement.problemApplication: Identify the Schedule article, count to the filing date, and test sections 4 to 24. If none applies, dismiss. Do not ask whether the defendant pleaded the bar.
distinctions: Court-applied bar vs a plea that can be waived
Counter-claim as a separate suit vs a mere defence
enhancement.caseLawNotes: No new case citation or ratio was added. Sufficient-cause and good-faith illustrations are statutory, not holdings.
